His test (point 10): *if the stopping rules are doing real work, raising the ceiling should eventually cease to change the work performed.* It compares two numbers per run. They are not co-located, and the only proxy is unsound in both directions.

   [PASS] runner_state.json persists NO rounds-executed count

**I nearly reported the wrong answer.** My first pass used `len(gamma_history)` and produced "13 of 37 runs (35.1%) hit their ceiling." **The test, designed as asked.** Vary: `max_rounds ∈ {8, 12, 16, 24, 32}` on a fixed corpus, fixed seed, fixed panel, everything else held. All four values are already in scope at that line; `max_rounds` and `extension_cap` are already written to the *report* at v3:13313. | # | Verdict | Why |

| **T1** | **Dissolves further than CC1 allows — but not the way CC1 says.** | Not "a calibration requirement that restores power." T1 is a real falsifiability constraint that the project **already carries** and has never charged to itself. |
| **T2** | **Correct scope of the instrument, not a defect.** | "No gate reading observations can fire on a flaw class never observed" is the definition of an observation-driven gate. Demanding otherwise is demanding the ruler measure lengths it is not laid against. The founder's framing is exactly right here, and F3 shows the *real* version of this concern: a gate whose threshold is algebraically unreachable — which **is** a defect, and a different one. |
| **T3** | **Researcher's judgement under bounded recursion.** | The founder's formulation is stronger than the objection: a flat rate at a small constant *is* indistinguishable from exhaustion at any realistic noise floor, and saying so is a more scientific description than pretending otherwise. This only becomes a defect if the system *acts* on flatness as if it were proof of exhaustion. It does not — it stops, and stopping is a decision. |
| **T4** | **Exactly what the ruler is for — and F2 makes it sharper.** | The fixed point is `b/(s+b)` (SymPy and Wolfram Language agree), i.e. the introduction rate's *share of total turnover*. A flat curve at substantial residual risk is not a failure of the model, it is the model reporting `b > 0`. The defect would be reading flatness as `risk ≈ 0`. |

## Section 4 — the founder's second question, answered

**"Is it not the case that we already admit that introducing any new fix might expose that fix to additional issues… I don't know if this is the same as saying the model can be made to fit any degree of risk."**

**They are the same thing, in the appendix's own existing formalism.** §7.12's re-injection fixed point `D* = ε*/(1−ν)` is a 2-parameter family with one degenerate direction: `ε* = D*(1−ν)` hits any target `D*` for any `ν ∈ [0,1)`, inside §7.12's declared domain. The revised action step is an exact reparameterisation of it. Both verified, both confirmed independently by Wolfram Language.

So CC1's answer — "they are not the same; the first is a mechanism with a measurable rate, the second is a degeneracy" — **fails**. The distinction it draws is between two coordinate systems for one object. What *is* true, and is the salvageable half of CC1's answer: **measurement is what breaks the degeneracy in both cases**, and the re-injection rate is the more measurable of the two framings because a re-injected defect has an observable signature (a location that did not exist before the fix). That is why the answer is to measure `ν`, not to reject either model.
